newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Look for EMU convergence,higher yields.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Look for EMU convergence,higher yields.

text.p: European bonds remain on track for convergence ahead of a punctual European economic and monetary union (EMU), but prices will soften, analysts said on Friday.

"We have convergence at lower yield levels now, but yields in core Europe will rise, and we will converge at higher levels," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
Italian bonds fell back from their recent highs on Friday, following comments late on Thursday by French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn.
Strauss-Kahn said for the first time that France would definitely not reach the Maastricht treaty target of limiting its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday stamped on talk of softening or delaying EMU.
He said that anyone who talked of a delay to the euro should know this could mean a permanent delay, and that the euro would be introduced fully in line with the Maastricht criteria.
Other European bonds held steady following Strauss-Kahn and Kohl's remarks, and the ten-year OAT/Bund spread also remained resilient.
"Two of the main players have reiterated their position," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International Europe.
"They have said nothing new."
French bonds can reach a negative yield spread of 15 basis points against Germany on a three-month horizon, from their current negative eight basis points, Brickman said.
"French bonds have held up because a cut in next year's deficit is expected, domestic demand is staying very strong, and the 10-year spread is not near its high," said McDevitt.
Strauss-Kahn said the 1997 deficit would not be three percent or 3.1 percent.

But French daily Liberation on Friday quoted an unnamed senior official saying France was aiming to reduce its deficit to 3.3 percent for 1997 and three percent for 1998. The French finance ministry declined to comment on the report.
"Strauss-Kahn's forecasts are hardly surprising when the market median is for a deficit of around 3.6 percent for 1997," said Brickman.

Bond convergence would only suffer if the latest round of comments was interpreted as increasing the likelihood of a delay to the EMU start date, said Jean-Francois Mercier, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
"But that risk looks moderate because of the French government's commitment to the start date. It scaled back its demands quite a bit to sign the stability pact in Amsterdam."
The French stance should help Italian bonds, despite their initial correction on Friday, economists said.
"Italy will benefit from a greater flexibility towards the treaty, though there are still question marks over whether it will make it into EMU first time around," said Brickman.

Italian government bonds hit a record low yield spread of 111 basis points against Bunds on Wednesday. The spread can travel in further, to 100 basis points on a three-month basis, Brickman said. It was quoted at 117 basis points at 1034 GMT.
But while a more lenient approach to budget deficits will benefit peripheral bond markets and therefore convergence, the impact on the core markets will be negative, analysts said.
"It is making people more aware of the weak euro scenario," said McDevitt.

Bunds have gained in recent days against Treasuries, with the 10-year spread widening to 92 basis points from 75 basis points. But the widening reflects short-term switching from Treasuries, rather than sustainable gains for Bunds, McDevitt said.
